data.title: Beijing to bar young 'red-chip' firms from listing outside mainland China, sources say
data.description:
Key points:
  • Red-chip firms must redomicile in China before they can list offshore, sources say
  • Red-chip firms are registered abroad but control assets and businesses in China
  • Beijing has been gradually tightening oversight of capital raising by red-chip firms

China's securities watchdog has told some law firms it will not approve plans by red-chip firms to list outside mainland China, people familiar with the matter said, a move that tightens its control of capital raised offshore and could dent Hong Kong's IPO market.

Red-chip companies are registered abroad, mainly in tax havens, but control assets and businesses in China via equity ownership or contractual agreements.

The structure is favoured by Chinese startups, particularly tech firms, keen to raise capital in places like Hong Kong or New York to take advantage of more relaxed rules and deeper pools of funds available from foreign investors.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) has told law firm representatives in recent days that red-chip companies established after the introduction of new offshore listing rules in 2023 must be re-domiciled in China before they can list offshore, said the people.

The people declined to be identified as the regulatory guidance was confidential. The move is being reported for the first time by Reuters.

China and the US are competing fiercely to gain the upper hand in tech, particularly in AI and semiconductors, which has led to efforts by Chinese authorities to sharpen their scrutiny of technology, data and capital going outside its borders.

The CSRC did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Oversight of red-chip firms has gradually become stricter.

Prior to March 2023, Chinese companies employing overseas holding structures to raise capital abroad did not need regulatory approval. That changed with the advent of the new rules.

Then this year, the CSRC told Reuters in March that it was examining the "necessity and compliance" of red-chip structures, particularly those formed after March 2023.

Despite that warning, some red-chip IPO hopefuls and their advisors have been seeking approval to list outside the mainland without dismantling their existing structure and shifting their domicile back to China, one of the people said.

Most of those applicants failed to convince the regulator that a red-chip structure was necessary, prompting the tougher stance, the person added.

HONG KONG IPO MARKET COULD BE HURT

A drop-off in listings from red-chip firms is likely to hurt but not hobble Hong Kong, the top IPO destination for Chinese firms, which has seen business boom for the past 18 months.

Funds raised via IPOs in Hong Kong during the first 10 months of this year surged 84% from the same period last year to hit HK$404 billion ($52 billion), though the CSRC has slowed approvals of IPOs since September.

In addition to going slow on approvals for listings by AI, chip and humanoid robot firms after a market frenzy in those sectors, it has more broadly increased its scrutiny as markets have weakened.

Last year, one-fifth of 131 Hong Kong listings approved by the CSRC involved offshore holdings, the majority of which used a red-chip structure, according to Chinese law firm Han Kun.

So far this year, the CSRC has approved Hong Kong listings for just 6 red-chip companies, a sharp decline from 50 approved last year, according to data compiled by law firms and Reuters.

There were nearly 600 listing applications pending in Hong Kong at the end of October, official data showed.

Most of them are mainland Chinese firms though it was not clear how many are red chips given that the number includes applications that were filed confidentially.

There are, however, at least four active Hong Kong IPO applicants which have an offshore holding company structure for their mainland China businesses, according to a Reuters review of filings with the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Any red-chip firms seeking to list in Hong Kong or New York could now face a long wait before coming to market due to the time and costs involved in becoming incorporated in China.

But some, like Chinese AI firm StepFun, have been working on shifting their domicile back to China to pave the way for a planned overseas listing, sources have said. StepFun did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Asked about news of the ban on red-chip firms listing outside mainland China, the Hong Kong bourse said it "welcomes issuers with a range of ownership structures, provided they meet all applicable regulatory requirements in Hong Kong and other relevant jurisdictions."

($1 = 7.8410 Hong Kong dollars)

data.title: Stock index futures rebound after AI wipeout
data.description:
Stock index futures popped Sunday night, signaling a potential positive open to start the week after the biggest selloff in years.

S&P 500 futures rose 0.76% to 6,963.05, while Nasdaq futures climbed 1.19% to 25,325.85. Dow futures advanced 0.61% to 48,442.28.

Last week, the S&P 500 (SP500) fell 8.6%, its biggest weekly drop since the April 2025 tariff crash, and it lost ground on all five trading days. The Dow lost 8%, its worst week since the COVID selloff of March 2020. And the Nasdaq Composite fell 10%, also its worst week since March 2020.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell about 17%, its worst week since the one following the September 11 attacks.

The Nasdaq is in the red for the year, while the S&P and Dow are now in correction territory for the first time since Liberation Day.

data.title: Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners Announces Sale of StraitNZ
data.description:
Morgan Stanley Investment Management (MSIM), through investment funds managed by Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners (MSIP), its private infrastructure investment platform, today announced it has entered into an agreement to sell StraitNZ (the Company), a New Zealand-based integrated transport, logistics and ferry company, to Partners Group, a leading global private markets firm, acting on behalf of its clients.

StraitNZ manages multiple daily freight and passenger services across the Cook Strait in New Zealand. StraitNZ is one of only two Cook Strait ferry operators, connecting New Zealand’s national highway system from the North Island to the South Island. Since MSIP’s investment in March 2022, the Company completed a full fleet refresh, introduced three-year CPI-linked take-or-pay freight contracts, rolled out dynamic passenger pricing, secured multi-decade port lease extensions and delivered strong EBITDA growth.

“StraitNZ demonstrates MSIP’s ability to identify high-quality essential infrastructure businesses and create value through active ownership and disciplined execution,” said Mark McLean, Managing Director and Co-Head of Asia-Pacific investing for MSIP. “Over our ownership period, we have worked alongside management to strengthen the Company’s commercial proposition, improve operational performance and position StraitNZ for sustainable long-term growth.”

Through its ferries and nationwide road freight network, StraitNZ provides an essential freight and passenger link, connecting customers, communities and businesses across New Zealand’s supply chain. Services are expected to continue as normal while the transaction is completed.

The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to customary regulatory approvals and other closing conditions.

About Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners

Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners (MSIP) is a leading global private infrastructure investment platform with approximately $17 billion in capital commitments since inception. Founded in 2006, MSIP has invested in a diverse portfolio across transportation, digital, energy transition, and water and waste. MSIP targets assets that provide essential public goods and services with the potential for value creation through active ownership. For further information about Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners, please visit Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners.

Morgan Stanley Investment Management

Morgan Stanley Investment Management, together with its investment advisory affiliates, has more than 1,300 investment professionals around the world and $2.1 trillion in assets under management or supervision as of September 30, 2026. Morgan Stanley Investment Management strives to provide outstanding long-term investment performance, service, and a comprehensive suite of investment management solutions to a diverse client base, which includes governments, institutions, corporations and individuals worldwide. For further information about Morgan Stanley Investment Management, please visit www.morganstanley.com/im.

About Morgan Stanley

Morgan Stanley () is a leading global financial services firm providing a wide range of investment banking, securities, wealth management and investment management services. With offices in 42 countries, the Firm’s employees serve clients worldwide including corporations, governments, institutions and individuals. For further information about Morgan Stanley, please visit www.morganstanley.com.

data.title: APL Apollo Tubes shares in focus after mega ₹28,000 crore deal with Tata Steel
data.description:
Shares of APL Apollo Tubes Ltd. will be in focus on Monday, November 23, after the company announced two major strategic acquisitions from Tata Steel Ltd., on Sunday evening.

APL Apollo Tubes, as per its exchange filing, will be acquiring Tata Steel's manufacturing, processing, marketing, sale and distribution of steel tubes and pipes business at its facilities in Jamshedpur, Hosur, Khopoli and Sahibabad, on a slump sale basis for ₹11,700 crore.

Additionally, the company will also be acquiring Tata Steel's 50% stake in its wholly-owned subsidiary Tata Steel Colors Pvt. Ltd., and its indirectly owned 50% stake in the company through another wholly-owned subsidiary Tata Steel Downstream Products Ltd., for a total consideration of ₹16,300 crore.

It remains to be seen how APL Apollo announces the funding of this transaction as the total consideration of ₹28,000 crore is well above the company's cash on the books at the end of the September quarter, which stood at only ₹1,600 crore. According to APL Apollo's filing, the consideration for both the transactions will be paid in cash upon completion.

The long stop date for both the transactions, under the share purchase agreement, has been fixed as March 31, 2028, subject to satisfaction of the conditions precedent set out in the SPA.

According to analysts, this could mean a significant expansion of APL Apollo's business footprint. The tubes business contributed to 4.9% of Tata Steel's overall consolidated revenue, while Tata Steel Colors contributed 2%.

At the end of financial year 2026, Tata Steel Colors had reported a topline of ₹4,680 crore, higher than the ₹4,234 crore reported in financial year 2025, and the ₹4,240 crore reported in financial year 2024. It reported a net profit of ₹85 crore in financial year 2026.

Shares of APL Apollo Tubes had ended 1.2% lower on Friday at ₹2,121.6. The stock has gained 4% in the last one month, taking its year-to-date advance to 7.7%.

data.title: Australia Business Conditions Contract at Fastest Pace in 5 Years
data.description:
By James Glynn

SYDNEY--Australian business conditions contracted at their fastest pace in five years in November, adding to concerns that the economy has slowed sharply following five interest rate rises since the start of 2026.

The headline seasonally adjusted S&P Global Flash Australia PMI composite output index remained below the 50.0 neutral mark for a second consecutive month in November. At 46.1--down from 48.2--the reading was the lowest since August 2021.

The decline was attributed to deeper contractions in output across both the manufacturing and service sectors, with the rates of decline the strongest in 25 and 36 months, respectively.

The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised interest rates aggressively in response to elevated inflation. The official cash rate now stands at 4.85%, its highest level in 18 years.

"November's flash PMI data revealed that Australia's business conditions deteriorated at the sharpest pace in more than five years as the reduction in new orders turned broad-based, with services new business now also in contraction," said Jingyi Pan, economics associate director at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

The PMI data followed last week's release of data showing unemployment jumped in October to 4.9%. Economists expect the RBA to hold rates at its next policy meeting in December.

"The latest decline in demand reflected the impact of higher interest rates, while softening domestic and external conditions also contributed," Pan said.

Inflationary pressures eased for the first time in several months as demand softened across the board, speaking to the effectiveness of the recent tightening of financial conditions, she added.

The data also showed employment fell alongside a marked reduction in business confidence among private-sector firms, pointing to more subdued near-term output conditions at a time when inflation has yet to be fully brought under control, Pan said.

-Write to James Glynn at james.glynn@wsj.com

data.title: OpenAI scientist proposes industry AI limits tied to model intelligence metric
data.description:
AI developers should adopt common limits on increasingly powerful models and use "perplexity" as a common metric for measuring AI progress across the industry, OpenAI's chief scientist said on Sunday in a proposal backed by CEO Sam Altman.

The proposal detailed by OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki in a blog post was unveiled at a time of growing concern inside and outside the industry about the potential risks of AI's rapidly growing capabilities.

"I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone," Pachocki wrote.

Pachocki described perplexity as a model intelligence metric concerning how well a model predicts the next token — the basic unit of data — on average, and wrote that lower perplexity means better predictions.

Pachocki wrote that AI could help drive fundamental advances in AI training methods as soon as 2027, potentially accelerating progress more quickly than advances in monitoring and safety. Developers should commit to not cross agreed capability thresholds until new monitoring and safety mechanisms are in place, Pachocki said.

Pachocki advocated for an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, and defines what milestones must be met before that limit is exceeded.

Altman backed the proposal, saying in a post on X that the industry should seek agreement on common limits for AI development. Altman described Pachocki's essay as "the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile," and said such limits would help ensure safety and control.

data.title: European steel makers ask Anglo-American, MMG for more safeguards
data.description:
European steel makers on Monday asked Anglo American and MMG for more safeguards to protect low-carbon ferronickel supply beyond the remedies offered by the two companies to get antitrust approval for the sale of a Brazil business.

"We recognise the efforts made by Anglo American and MMG to address the concerns raised, and the revised commitments are a positive step," said Axel Eggert, the Director General of Eurofer, which represents the steel makers of the European Union and other countries.

More measures are needed to ensure that stainless steel makers in the region have access to the raw material, he added.

Anglo American and MMG are seeking the approval of the $500 million sale of Anglo American's ferronickel mining operation in Brazil by the European Commission, which acts as the antitrust regulator for the EU.

Adjustments to MMG's proposed remedies include increasing the volumes of ferronickel supplied to Europe to 16,000 metric tons a year from 11,500 tons and providing greater certainty over contracts and pricing flexibility, said a person close to the talks.

Steelmakers fear the crucially low-carbon ferronickel from Brazil, which is produced with hydropower, could be diverted to other areas than Europe after the sale.

The Commission, which is leaning towards a veto, is set to decide on the deal by December 21.

Anglo American last month said it would close down the ferronickel business were the sale blocked by the antitrust regulator.
